etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English tak, takke (“hook; staple; nail”), from Old Northern French taque (“nail, pin, peg”), from Frankish *takkō, from Proto-Germanic *takkô (“tip; point; protrusion; prong; tine; jag; spike; twig”), of unknown origin, but possibly from Proto-Indo-European *dHgʰ-n-, from the root *déHgʰ- (“to pinch; to tear, rip, fray”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Takke (“bough; branch; twig”), West Frisian takke (“branch”), tûk (“branch, smart, sharp”), Dutch tak (“twig; branch; limb”), German Zacke (“jag; prong; spike; tooth; peak”).

definitions.definition: A small nail with a flat head.

quote.citation: 2012 July 15, Richard Williams, “Tour de France 2012: Carpet tacks cannot put Bradley Wiggins off track”, in The Guardian‎[1]:
quote.text: A tough test for even the strongest climber, it was new to the Tour de France this year, but its debut will be remembered for the wrong reasons after one of those spectators scattered carpet tacks on the road and induced around 30 punctures among the group of riders including Bradley Wiggins, the Tour's overall leader, and his chief rivals.

definitions.definition: A thumbtack.
(sewing) A loose seam used to temporarily fasten pieces of cloth.
(nautical) The lower corner on the leading edge of a sail relative to the direction of the wind.
(nautical) A course or heading that enables a sailing vessel to head upwind.
(figurative) A direction or course of action, especially a new one; a method or approach to solving a problem.

quote.citation: 1612, Michael Drayton, chapter 11, in [John Selden], editor, Poly-Olbion. Or A Chorographicall Description of Tracts, Riuers, Mountaines, Forests, and Other Parts of this Renowned Isle of Great Britaine, […], London:  […]  H[umphrey] L[ownes] for Mathew Lownes; I[ohn] Browne; I[ohn] Helme; I[ohn] Busbie, published 1613, →OCLC:
quote.text: So stoutly held to tack by those near North-wales men;

quote.citation: 1922 February, James Joyce, “[V]”, in Ulysses, Paris: Shakespeare and Company, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Maud Gonne’s letter about taking them off O’Connell street at night: disgrace to our Irish capital. Griffith’s paper is on the same tack now: an army rotten with venereal disease: overseas or halfseasover empire.

quote.citation: 1994, Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom: The Autobiography of Nelson Mandela, London: Abacus, published 2010, page 637:
quote.text: I thought that my refusing Barnard would alienate Botha, and decided that such a tack was too risky.

quote.citation: 2016 June 19, Mary Dejevsky, “Isolating Russia isn’t working. The west needs a new approach”, in The Guardian‎[2]:
quote.text: When even cautious German politicians are questioning Nato’s ‘war-mongering’ actions, it’s clear that a new tack is required

definitions.definition: (nautical) The maneuver by which a sailing vessel turns its bow through the wind so that the wind changes from one side to the other.
(nautical) The distance a sailing vessel runs between these maneuvers when working to windward; a board.
(nautical) A rope used to hold in place the foremost lower corners of the courses when the vessel is close-hauled; also, a rope employed to pull the lower corner of a studding sail to the boom.
Any of the various equipment and accessories worn by horses in the course of their use as domesticated animals.
(manufacturing, construction, chemistry) The stickiness of a compound, related to its cohesive and adhesive properties.

quote.citation: 1959, E. A. Apps, Printing Ink Technology, page 415:
quote.text: Letterpress and offset gloss varnishes normally have viscosities varying from 50 to 250 poises; they must stain the paper as little as possible, have insufficient tack to cause plucking,  […]

definitions.definition: Food generally; fare, especially of the bread kind.

quote.citation: 1913, D[avid] H[erbert] Lawrence, Sons and Lovers, London: Duckworth & Co. […], →OCLC:
quote.text: But if a woman's got nothing but her fair fame to feed on, why, it's thin tack, and a donkey would die of it!

definitions.definition: That which is attached; a supplement; an appendix.

quote.citation: a. 1716 (date written), [Gilbert] Burnet, edited by [Gilbert Burnet Jr.], Bishop Burnet’s History of His Own Time. […], volume (please specify |volume=I or II), London:  […]  Thomas Ward […], published 1724, →OCLC:
quote.text: Some tacks had been made to money bills in King Charles's time.

quote.citation: 1849–1861, Thomas Babington Macaulay, The History of England from the Accession of James the Second, volume (please specify |volume=I to V), London: Longman, Brown, Green, and Longmans, →OCLC:
quote.text: pay all taxes and subscribe tacks

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Confidence; reliance.

quote.citation: 1651-1666, Joseph Caryl, Exposition of Job with Practical Observations:
quote.text: He should find […] that there was tack in it, that it was solid silver, or silver that had strength in it.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English takken (“to attach; nail”), from the noun (see above).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To nail (something) with a tack (small nail with a flat head).
To sew/stitch with a tack (loose seam used to temporarily fasten pieces of cloth).
To weld with initial small welds to temporarily fasten in preparation for full welding.
(nautical) To maneuver a sailing vessel so that its bow turns through the wind, i.e. the wind changes from one side of the vessel to the other.
(intransitive, nautical) To sail to windward using a series of alternate tacks across the wind.
To add something as an extra item.

quote.citation: 2012, James Lambert, “Beyond Hobson-Jobson: A new lexicography for Indian English”, in World Englishes‎[3], page 312:
quote.text: In short, they tend to present Indian English as nothing more than "standard" English with a select collection of lexical peculiarities tacked on, as it were, many of which would be regarded as "errors" by prescriptivist language scholars.

definitions.definition: Synonym of tack up (“to prepare a horse for riding by equipping it with a tack”).
(slang, obsolete) To join in wedlock.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From an old or dialectal form of French tache. See techy. Doublet of tache.

definitions.definition: A stain; a tache.
(obsolete) A peculiar flavour or taint.
(colloquial) That which is tacky; something cheap and gaudy.

quote.citation: 2014, David Leffman, The Rough Guide to China:
quote.text: For souvenirs – mostly outright tack and ethnicky textiles – try your bargaining skills at the shops and stalls on Binjiang Luand Zhengyang Jie, or the nightly street market spreading for about a block either side of Shanhu Bridge along Zhongshan Lu.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English tak, take (“fee, tax (on livestock)”), from Old Norse tak, taka (“a taking, seizure; revenue”), from Old Norse taka (“to take”). Cognate with Scots tack.

definitions.definition: (law, Scotland and Northern England) A contract by which the use of a thing is set, or let, for hire; a lease.

quote.citation: 1885, Lord Colin Campbell, The Crofter in History:
quote.text: In the Breadalbane papers, for example, there is a "tack" which was given by Sir John Campbell of Glenurchy to his "weil belouit" servant John M'Conoquhy V'Gregour, in the year 1530.
